title: Threat Modeling AI Systems
description: Study assets, actors and trust boundaries, attack surfaces and misuse cases, risk prioritization and impact, and security invariants and acceptance tests. Each lesson includes a worked example and an applied practice task.

lessons.title: Assets, actors and trust boundaries
lessons.description: Draw the data flow and mark where refund authority is granted.
lessons.conceptOverview: Threat modeling identifies valuable assets, possible adversaries and boundaries where data or authority changes hands. Include model inputs, retrieved content, tools and stored artifacts rather than treating the model as the entire system.
lessons.whyItMatters: Security analysis must include tool authority and data flows.

sections.title: Worked example

keyTakeaways: Security analysis must include tool authority and data flows.
commonMistakes: Only model weights matter in an AI threat model.

lessons.title: Attack surfaces and misuse cases
lessons.description: Write the input, trust crossing and unauthorized action in this misuse case.
lessons.conceptOverview: An attack surface includes uploads, retrieval sources, tool arguments, dependencies and outputs. Describe misuse cases as concrete sequences with preconditions and impact so defenses can be tested.
lessons.whyItMatters: Concrete attack paths support testable defenses.

lessons.title: Risk prioritization and impact
lessons.description: Compare the impacts and choose which control to implement first.
lessons.conceptOverview: Prioritize threats using plausible likelihood, exposure and consequence. A low-frequency unauthorized transaction can deserve more attention than a common harmless formatting error.
lessons.whyItMatters: Risk prioritization must consider consequence, not just frequency.

lessons.title: Security invariants and acceptance tests
lessons.description: Write an authorization invariant and test it during retry and recovery.
lessons.conceptOverview: An invariant is a property that must hold across all workflow paths, such as no cross-tenant retrieval or no write without authorization. Turn invariants into tests at enforcement boundaries.
lessons.whyItMatters: Security invariants must hold on failure paths too.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: An invariant is a property that must hold across all workflow paths, such as no cross-tenant retrieval or no write without authorization. Turn invariants into tests at enforcement boundaries.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A refund workflow is tested only on the ordinary approval path, leaving its retry path unchecked.

sections.title: Practice & verification
sections.content: Write an authorization invariant and test it during retry and recovery. Write down your reasoning and check it against the concept before continuing.

keyTakeaways: Security invariants must hold on failure paths too.
commonMistakes: Testing the happy path establishes complete authorization safety.
